entities.summary:
A banknote is a promissory note issued by a bank, now typically a central bank, that functions as legal tender — a form of currency that by law must be accepted for settlement of debts. Banknotes replaced commodity money (gold, silver coins) as the primary medium of exchange in most economies, and their issuance is fundamental to modern monetary systems and central banking.

The earliest banknotes appeared in Tang dynasty China (7th century CE) as 'flying money' (fei-qian) — deposit receipts for merchants who wished to avoid carrying heavy coin across long distances. The Jiaozi of Song dynasty China (10th–13th centuries) became the first government-issued paper currency. In Europe, the first banknotes appeared in the 17th century: the Stockholm Banco issued credit notes in 1661; the Bank of England (founded 1694) issued notes that became the model for modern central bank currency.

The transition from commodity-backed currency to fiat money — currency whose value rests entirely on government authority and public trust — was a profound economic transformation. The gold standard, under which notes were redeemable for gold, operated through much of the 19th and early 20th centuries. The United States abandoned the gold standard in 1971 (Nixon shock), completing the global transition to pure fiat currency. Today's banknotes incorporate advanced security features (holograms, microprinting, specialized inks) to prevent counterfeiting, and their role is being challenged by digital payment systems and central bank digital currencies (CBDCs).
